vignette:
Tane was forty-seven when the accident happened. He had been working in community organizing for over a decade by then, running youth outreach programs in South Auckland, and he was good at the work—the kind of man who showed up, who listened, who made young people feel seen. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, he was driving a van full of teenagers back from a field trip to a local environmental center. The rain had come down hard that morning, and the roads were still slick. He remembered the sky clearing. He remembered a radio announcement. Then there was nothing—a gap like someone had taken scissors to the film of his life. When consciousness returned, he was upside down, metal screaming, the smell of fuel and something else, something like copper. A boy was crying. Tane's right leg was pinned. The next clear image was a police officer's face through the broken window, then the sound of the jaws of life, then pain so sharp it seemed to split him open. Three teenagers had been injured. None had died. Tane had spent eight weeks in hospital. Now, at sixty-three, sixteen years had passed since that Tuesday, and the distance of time had done almost nothing to dull the weight of what he carried.

The physical recovery had taken months. The psychological one, he had come to understand, might never finish. The middle section of the accident—the moment of impact itself—remained sealed off, inaccessible. He knew intellectually what must have happened: the van had hydroplaned, crossed the centerline, struck a utility vehicle head-on. But he could not access the sensory reality of it, could not find the words to describe even what he did remember. When he tried to talk about it in those early years, his mouth would open and close like a fish pulled from water. Eventually he stopped trying. What he could not stop were the thoughts. They arrived unbidden and unwelcome—images of the teenagers' faces, scenarios in which the outcome had been different, darker. The thoughts felt like intrusions, like something pressing against his skull from the inside. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt immovable, that the accident had been his fault. He had been driving. He had made the decision to take that route. He had not anticipated the rain. The logic was circular and airtight: if he had acted differently—left earlier, chosen a different road, driven slower—those young people would not have been in danger. The fact that they had survived did not absolve him; it only meant he had been lucky, and luck was not the same as innocence.

Over the years, Tane had constructed a careful architecture of avoidance that had slowly contracted the boundaries of his life. He no longer drove; the moment he sat behind a steering wheel, his hands would begin to shake uncontrollably, and his vision would narrow as though the world were closing in. He took the bus, walked, or accepted rides from colleagues, though fewer colleagues remained willing to offer them as he became less present at work. He stopped attending community events where police or security personnel might be present in uniform; the sight of that blue or black fabric, the badge and belt, sent his heart into a gallop and made his palms sweat in a way he could not control. His body, he had come to feel, was a traitor—it reacted as if danger were imminent even when he sat safely in his living room. Sometimes his leg would twitch involuntarily, or his chest would tighten, and he would think: *there is nothing happening, but my body does not believe that*. The disconnect was profound. He felt dead inside, as though the part of him that could feel joy or connection had been severed in that moment of impact and had never regenerated. He experienced a persistent numbness that made even his favorite foods taste like cardboard, made conversations feel like he was speaking through thick glass. Food itself had become a chore; he ate because he knew he had to, not because anything brought him pleasure.

Most difficult was his response to anger in others. When a colleague raised their voice in a meeting, even with legitimate frustration about a funding delay, Tane's nervous system would flood with alarm. His hands would shake. He would excuse himself. Over time, he began avoiding meetings where conflict might arise, then avoiding colleagues who seemed prone to intensity, then avoiding the office altogether. His supervisor had gently suggested he might consider part-time work, then eventually part-time had become a medical leave, then early retirement. The irony was not lost on him: a man whose life's work was community building had become increasingly isolated, increasingly unreachable. When he moved to Wellington at fifty-five, telling himself it was for a fresh start, it was really to remove himself entirely from the world he had built. His colleagues had stopped calling after the first year. His sister sent cards at Christmas that he would read once and place in a drawer, unable to find the words to respond.

At sixty-three, Tane sat in his small apartment in Wellington, where the light came in gray through the windows overlooking the harbor, and admitted to himself that something had to change. The isolation was complete now. The unwanted thoughts had become louder, more vivid, arriving with a clarity that felt almost hallucinatory—he could see the teenagers' faces with such precision that he would sometimes check his phone to make sure he was in the present moment and not somehow back in that van. His body's betrayals had become more frequent and more severe; sometimes his heart would race for hours with no trigger he could identify, or his leg would twitch so violently that he would stumble. He had finally called a therapist because he could no longer live inside the architecture he had built. He was afraid that talking about it would make it real in a way that silence had prevented, that speaking the details aloud would somehow unlock the sealed-off moment of impact and flood him with sensations he was not sure he could survive. But he was more afraid of spending the rest of his life as a ghost in his own life—numb, trapped, unable to move toward anything or anyone. At sixty-three, he was running out of time to become a person again.
